image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted vertical bar chart** (group of small-multiple bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples**: three side-by-side panels for **U.S.**, **E.U.**, and **CHINA**.  
   - Bars are **not stacked**.  
   - All panels share a common time axis style and comparable percentage scale.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Electric models as percentage of total passenger vehicle sales | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Region / market (U.S., E.U., China) | Categorical/Nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel labels |
| Region highlight/status | Categorical/Nominal | Color/hue of bars (orange for U.S., light gray for E.U. and China) |

Notes:
- The title and subtitle indicate the measured quantity is the **share of electric models in total passenger vehicle sales**.
- Visible labels include percentage reference marks (e.g., 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%), which function as axis/grid annotations rather than separate data variables.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that China seemed to start later, but it has the highest percentage, whereas America started first, and yet has the smallest percentage. I also notice how America has a more wobbly effect to its graph much more than the other two graphs. America is the first to start using electric cars, yet it doesn't seem to have changed that much over the last decade. 

2. I wonder why America is so slow. Are we going to have a spike soon, or is it going to take a long time to reach where China or even E.U is at? I would think that it is probably due to how we have Uber and other rent-a-car facilities, meaning that a lot of people don't really need a car for themselves. I am curious how people haven't made the switch, and wonder if it is because they aren't as available in stores, or if they are more expensive. I would think, however, that since gas prices are so high, people would be more willing to switch. 

3. This affects my community because of how much healthier it could be if we used electric cars. I believe that if we switch to electric, it would be much easier for people with lung problems, like myself, to deal with since there wouldn't be as much exhaust. I am also curious if it would help lower people's car bills with gas since its heightened price these days. If we switch, I think we would have a more efficient way to travel. 

4. The Electric Car, is it Really Going That Far?

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   

Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: "Headline: America running on gas, can't keep up with the electric car movement." by Grace at Academy of Saint Elizabeth in New Jersey, “The U.S. Falls Behind in the Race of Electric Vehicle Sales” by Max of Eleanor Roosevelt High School in New York City and “Electric Car Takeover in Europe and China! The U.S. Trying to Catch Up” by Carlos of Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey.  Note that these headlines focus on comparing the electric car sales taking over car sales with the US lagging.  This is what is so surprising about these graphs. 

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free links to the articles that include these graphs.  Also in the Reveal are a summary of the topic, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph. 

The next graph will be released by Friday, Oct. 27, but the moderation will be Wednesday, Nov. 8 – in two weeks.   Hope to read your responses next week when the topic will be YOUR college rankings.  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who just bought a hybrid SUV and loves the “free” fuel and not going to the gas station as often, and Beth Anne Merida of New Orleans, who hadn't considered buying an electric vehicle until now.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph represents the percentage of car purchases that were fully electric vehicles from 2010 to 2022. From 2010 to 2016, the percentage of electric cars purchased from the U.S., E.U., and China, were all under 5%. After 2016, the purchase of electric cars began to increase drastically. As of 2022, the percentage of vehicles purchased in China that were EVs came to just under 30%. As for the E.U., their purchase percentage of EVs for 2022 was just above 20%, while the U.S. stays low coming in under 10%. I wonder what was the sudden boom for Chinese electric vehicle purchasers between 2020 and 2021 considering the total percentage rose around 10%. With COVID-19 still being very apparent and production being slow globally, how was the Chinese population receiving these cars? In my community, I see the rise of electric cars more and more every day. Because of rising gas prices and the amount of driving my parents do due to work, in the past year my family has purchased two fully electric cars. I know that other families in my area, with most adults commuting into New York City for work, have turned to electric or hybrid vehicles for their long-term cost-effectiveness. On my annual trip to the West Coast to visit family, electric vehicles have completely taken over on that side of the United States. Which, I assume, is due to the close proximity to Silicon Valley. 

“We Watt Electric Cars!”

comments.raw_comment: I notice that electric cars are more popular in China than in Europe and the US. They have significantly more usage now, despite their lower percentage of usage 10 years ago. It does seem that China is also a large country, with a similar production structure so it would make sense that the US and China would have similar percentages of Electric car sales. comments.raw_comment:
I notice that these bar graphs depict the rise in sales of electric cars through the years for the US, the European Union, and China. The biggest percent increases have occurred in the most recent years (approximately 2019-2022). Additionally, the EU and China have both seen exponential growth in their sales, while sales in the United States have grown linearly. 

I wonder why China and the European Union have substantially more electric car sales than the United States, despite the US being one of the top car manufacturing countries, second only to China (OICA 2021). I wonder if it's because of the different incentives some countries offer to owners of electric cars. For example, in the EU, electric car drivers pay no purchase taxes or VAT on electric cars, benefit from free parking, and are exempt from all road tolls. Additionally, China unveiled a 520 billion yuan package of tax breaks over four years for electric vehicles (EVs) and other green cars. 

This affects my community because, as a citizen of the United States, I worry about the environmental impact my country has on the world. Without incentives like the ones in the EU and China, many in the US cannot afford electric or hybrid cars, as they are generally more expensive than regular gas cars. This not only gives the US a reputation for high pollution, but it also causes a disproportionate amount of air pollution in lower-income areas, which can lead to health hazards. 

Title: The US Left in the Dust?

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice:
Upon the first glance of this graph, I noticed the extreme increase in sales of all the places on the graph between 2021 to 2022, especially with China, making me think that maybe it was the marketing tactics or just positive reviews on this vehicle that really boosted the sales.
What do I wonder?
I wonder how this data will change in the next 10 years or so. As many locations are installing charging ports, which may potentially boost the amount of sales by a lot since a primary factor of owning a vehicle is the convenience in maintaining them. In addition, I wonder how international places like China will grow in sales, seeing as they have already had a stark increase in sales--Will this hype be sustainable as the years go on?
How does this affect my community?
As our society has reached the pivotal transition in the transportation industry, making electric vehicles have a fresh, new feel to how we transport ourselves, it is important that we take a step back from what we immediately want in a given moment and do some research about how your country is reacting to the new phenomenon since electric vehicles can potentially be dangerous to those who do not know how to use them correctly. Therefore, it's important to see through a general lens how a whole range of people in a country choose to spend their money on these vehicles. 
Society has really been struck by electric vehicles

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, the exponential growth in electrical vehicle sales is detailed. It is separated into countries, and it shows the growth of electric car sales between 2010 and 2022 in each country respectively. The graph shows a spike in electric car sales, beginning in 2020 in every country. The total percentage of cars sold that are electric is largest in China, where in 2022, nearly 30% of all passenger vehicle purchases were electric vehicles. In the US, only about 7-8% of car sales are electric cars, and in the E.U., a little over 20% of sales are electric cars. This spike could be caused by increasing awareness and panic over global warming and climate issues, so people could be rushing to buy vehicles that are better for the planet. This spike could also be caused by a rise in gas prices or the possibility of a more efficient and less expensive vehicle to maintain. I would name this graph: Electric Cars: Will You Hop on the Bandwagon?

1. In 2022, electric car-buying was at its greatest, having doubled from the year before in the US and China. In China, electric cars take up over 1/4 of total car sales, so maybe they have more brands or their electric cars are more affordable. If this trend continues, Europe and China will be dependent on electric cars in a few more years. Only 10 years ago, electric car sales were nearly 0, which shows how fast technology spreads and becomes popular over the course of only a decade.

2. I wonder why China's percentage of electric car sales is so high. I generally think of China as being polluted because of all the factories, so maybe people are trying to do something to help the environment. For electric cars to become more popular in the US, I wonder if there would need to be more charging stations in the middle of the country where it is all cornfields and plains. I wonder if the governments are pushing for more electric cars as part of the carbon-free, anti-climate change plans that are going on.

3. In communities with more electric cars, there is less car pollution, making them a cleaner place to live. Electric car sales, I assume, coincide with the wealth of a community because these cars are more expensive. This could increase the disparity between poor communities and rich communities where rich people can afford to live in a place with cleaner air. 

4. Revving up for an Electric Car Future

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Today’s graphs display the electric auto sales as percentages of total passenger vehicle sales in the U.S., the European Union and China.  How do these countries compare regarding electric car sales?  What is similar and what is different?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  If your notice includes a claim, please back it up with evidence that supports your claim.  

Remember to share with us your catchy headline which captures the main idea of the graphs.  We will give shout outs to some of the best headlines submitted before 2 pm ET today.  Get published in the New York Times Learning Network!  

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs.  

You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next graph will be released by Friday, Oct. 27.  Hope to read your responses next week when the topic will be YOUR college rankings.

Therefore, electric cars weren't being produced as much and they also weren't in high demand at the time. From this graph, we can see that China has the highest percentage of electric cars purchased. Is the government there encouraging people to go electric to reduce fossil fuels into the air?
"The World Will Run on Electric"

1. I notice that while Europe and China have majorly increased in sales (over 20%) over the past couple years, the US has only had a slight increase in sales (5% to 10%). From this information, I believe that we can come to a conclusion that US citizens are less likely to follow trends and buy these stylish cars than European citizens and Chinese citizens are. American citizens may also have a tendency to stick to their "traditional" ways while European and Chinese citizens are more open to ideas of innovation.

2. I wonder if it is just an idea of trends or if it is also a factor of money. Perhaps, American citizens don't believe that electric cars are worth the money and so they decide to put their income into something else while Chinese and European citizens believe that purchasing electric cars is a fine financial decision. Also, is it possible that there are not enough amenities in the US for electric cars, while there are gas stations everywhere?

3. I know that my parents who are American citizens do not like electric cars that much due to the fact that you have to charge them. They've heard horror stories of these cars running out of battery and my mom drove one once and she said it gave her a lot of anxiety trying to not run out of battery. 

4. My headline would be: "The Rising Popularity of Electric Cars & If These Trendy Vehicles Are Really Worth It"
